candidates.exact_span: The following Minimum Quantification Levels (MQL's) are to be used for reporting pollutant data for NPDES permit applications and/or compliance reporting.
candidates.computation_change_reason: Whether MQLs govern only application submittals, only compliance reporting, or both affects which reported measurements are in scope for limit comparison (A), which reporting obligations attach to monitored parameters (B), and how sub-MQL or non-quantified results are classified versus truly missing evidence (C). The 'and/or' scope is not resolved within this segment.

All tabulated MQL values are denominated in µg/l; a different unit interpretation (or failure to align reported measurements and permit limits to µg/l) would change numeric exceedance determinations (A) and whether a reported or non-detect value is treated as an ordinary numeric result versus a below-quantification state (C).

Two distinct MQL values appear for Mercury with a footnote marker (*1) whose operative meaning is not given in this segment; choosing 0.0005 versus 0.005 µg/l changes how mercury results are reported, whether a value is treated as quantified, and any numeric comparison against an applicable mercury limit (A), and whether a result is documented below quantification versus lacking adequate evidence (C).

This segment lists a separate MQL for weak-acid-dissociable cyanide distinct from total cyanide (MQL 10 µg/l each); applying the wrong cyanide MQL or analyte definition would change limit-exceedance handling for cyanide measurements (A) and classification of non-detect or sub-MQL cyanide results (C).

Residual chlorine is a regulated parameter class often subject to numeric limits; the stated MQL of 33 µg/l determines whether reported chlorine data are treated as quantified for compliance comparison (A) or as below-quantification/missing-evidence cases when results are reported below that level (C).

Dioxin congeners are typically subject to very low numeric limits; the extremely low MQL (0.00001 µg/l) affects whether measured or reported dioxin values can be numerically compared to an applicable limit (A) and whether results reported as less than quantification are distinguished from other no-data states (C).
